items.title: Sharon Armstrong, Ontario Stone, Sand & Gravel Association
notes:
S. Armstrong provided technical information related to the process of pumping water in aggregate operations. A copy of the presentation is attached to the addendum agenda.

Responding to Council, S. Armstrong explained that the water in quarries, similar to the one location in Puslinch, is clean. She explained that the filtration system takes impurities out of the water, and plants and fish are added to assist in rehabilitation of pits and quarries. 

Responding to Council, Stan Denhoed, Hydrogeologist, provided clarification related to water taking permits. He explained that the 9.7 million/L is not being taken from the aquifer it's the amount of water being pumped - 92% of water is retained in the closed-loop system. S. Denhoed explained that it is the pump and the volume on the pump that are required on the application, not the amount of water that is taken. 

Council expressed concern related to potential impact to water aquifers and the possibility of pits not being rehabilitated.

items.title: Other Matters Under Committee Of The Whole
EES-WIM-26-004, Mannheim Service Area Water Capacity Constraint - Clarifying Information
notes:
Amy Shaw, Director of Water and Wastewater Operations, introduced Ryan Snider, Manager of Water Operations and Management.  R. Snider provided a presentation with clarifying information related to the Mannheim Service Area Water Capacity Constraint. A copy of the presentation is attached to the addendum agenda. 

R. Snider provided a water system overview that includes nineteen (19) regulated water sub-systems in various forms such as fifty (50) Water treatment facilities and fifteen (15) pumping stations. He summarized the sustainable capacity and operational resilience.

Geoff Moroz, Manager of Hydrogeology & Water Programs, explained the supply risks associated with over-pumping or "peaking". G. Moroz explained that since 2021, the declining aquafer levels in Manheim have gotten close to the trigger level, which is the point in which private well water supplies would be impacted. He explained the increasing trend is due to over-pumping, which causes a gradual decline in water levels in the Manheim aquafer. 

R. Snider explained the operational impacts of peaking, including wear and damage to equipment, planned and unplanned shutdowns, and increasing infrastructure deficit. 

R. Reiger provided an update on the current state of development in the Middleton and Manheim Services Areas. He gave a brief overview of the potential of preliminary solutions to add up to 600+ L/s capacity by 2032. 

Wayne Steffler, Commissioner of Corporate Services, provided an update on the financial resources in the Water Capital Reserve ($102M) and the Water Development Charges Capital Reserve ($5.3M). In response to Council, W. Steffler confirmed that reserve funds are sufficient to cover the near-term plans, but requires action to ensure future needs are met. 

In response to Council, G. Moroz clarified a miscommunication that water is not being discharged to the ditch during stress testing, and is instead being sent to system. This has been ongoing since 2019. 

Council requested to see a full picture of the water situation in Wilmot. In response to Council, G. Moroz explained that through stressing testing, a more accurate inisght into the strain on the Region's water system has been captured. He stated that work to provide information on a wellfield-by-wellfield basis is ongoing.

Responding to a question from Council, G. Moroz stated that water levels in the Wilmot area are much higher than in Manheim and taking water will not result in drying up wells. G. Moroz clarified the proposed motion is not to take more water from Wilmot, but to establish the current levels being taken as permanent. G. Moroz confirmed the proposed 30 L/s to be taken from the total 135 L/s Wilmot pumps is extra and not used within the Wilmot area.

In response to Council, G. Moroz stated he is confident the tools used today would identify trends in water levels sooner than in the past.

Council requested a provincial tracking reports going back to 2022 and a report that would show the full picture of wellfields in the entire region. G. Moroz stated this can be provided by the next scheduled Council Meeting on March 25, 2026.

motions.item_title: EES-WIM-26-003, Optimizing the Sustainable Use of Water Resources for Municipal Supply (1980 Policy on Water Taking - Wilmot Township)
motions.text: Motion Referred That Council temporarily suspend the 1980 Council Wilmot Water Take Policy, rather than revoke it, until the Region’s new Water Supply Strategy is completed and presented to Council in 2027; That Council formally review the status of the 1980 policy upon receipt of the Water Supply Strategy in 2027, prior to making any permanent determination respecting revocation; That upon initiation of any increased draw from Wilmot wells , staff provide regular public reporting to Regional Council and the public, at a minimum quarterly, including but not limited to: total volume of water being taken; peak flow data; well performance indicators; aquifer health and drawdown monitoring data; commentary on whether continued suspension remains appropriate based on observed conditions; That staff establish and implement a monitoring framework to collect and publicly report data regarding: neighbouring private wells; surface water systems; agricultural water supply conditions; and any observed correlations associated with increased regional draw; That staff provide Council and the public with a clear definition of “surplus water” as used in Regional staff's SID Feb. 10 report on the 1980 water take policy, including: the modelling methodology applied; growth and demand assumptions used; safety factors and contingency thresholds; and alignment with Provincial permitting requirements; That staff provide clarification regarding the basis of the current statement that Wilmot’s growth to 2051 will not be impacted , including: the population and employment forecasts being used; the land use assumptions underlying those forecasts; the infrastructure modelling methodology applied; and the treatment of post-2051 growth within long-term supply planning; That the forthcoming Water Supply Strategy clearly distinguish between water allocation assumptions for Wilmot’s planned residential and employment growth and any projected demand associated with the Region’s designated Mega Site , including: the range of potential end-user water demand scenarios being modelled for the mega site; the planning assumptions being used in the absence of a confirmed end user; and the implications of those assumptions for long-term regional water allocation and that the mega site water use is independent of the guaranteed allocations for Wilmot's planned growth as per their 2026 Official Plan And that prior to implementation, Council be provided written confirmation that all applicable provincial permits and regulatory approvals required to support the increased water taking have been obtained
motions.text_html:
Motion Referred

  1. That Council temporarily suspend the 1980 Council Wilmot Water Take Policy, rather than revoke it, until the Region’s new Water Supply Strategy is completed and presented to Council in 2027;
  2. That Council formally review the status of the 1980 policy upon receipt of the Water Supply Strategy in 2027, prior to making any permanent determination respecting revocation;
  3. That upon initiation of any increased draw from Wilmot wells, staff provide regular public reporting to Regional Council and the public, at a minimum quarterly, including but not limited to:
  • total volume of water being taken;
  • peak flow data;
  • well performance indicators;
  • aquifer health and drawdown monitoring data;
  • commentary on whether continued suspension remains appropriate based on observed conditions;
  1. That staff establish and implement a monitoring framework to collect and publicly report data regarding:
    • neighbouring private wells;
    • surface water systems;
    • agricultural water supply conditions;
    • and any observed correlations associated with increased regional draw;
  2. That staff provide Council and the public with a clear definition of “surplus water” as used in Regional staff's SID Feb. 10 report on the 1980 water take policy, including:
    • the modelling methodology applied;
    • growth and demand assumptions used;
    • safety factors and contingency thresholds;
    • and alignment with Provincial permitting requirements;
  3. That staff provide clarification regarding the basis of the current statement that Wilmot’s growth to 2051 will not be impacted, including:
    • the population and employment forecasts being used;
    • the land use assumptions underlying those forecasts;
    • the infrastructure modelling methodology applied;
    • and the treatment of post-2051 growth within long-term supply planning;
  4. That the forthcoming Water Supply Strategy clearly distinguish between water allocation assumptions for Wilmot’s planned residential and employment growth and any projected demand associated with the Region’s designated Mega Site, including:
    • the range of potential end-user water demand scenarios being modelled for the mega site;
    • the planning assumptions being used in the absence of a confirmed end user;
    • and the implications of those assumptions for long-term regional water allocation and that the mega site water use is independent of the guaranteed allocations for Wilmot's planned growth as per their 2026 Official Plan
  5. And that prior to implementation, Council be provided written confirmation that all applicable provincial permits and regulatory approvals required to support the increased water taking have been obtained

motions.text: The Administration and Finance Committee recommends as follows: 1. That the Regional Municipality of Waterloo direct Facilities staff to explore the development of a Facilities Strategic Plan focused on the following five components: A complete inventory of all corporate facilities, including current usage, functional capacity, and condition; An analysis of operating and maintenance requirements and associated costs across all corporate facilities; A five- to ten-year capital outlook identifying required investments, lifecycle needs, and projected financial impacts; A review of accommodation standards and policies to support facilities planning and a demand analysis to clarify space needs; An evaluation of optimization opportunities, including consolidation, repurposing, or alternative service delivery options to ensure efficient and cost-effective use of corporate space; And that staff report back to Council with the findings, options, and recommended next steps. 2. The Council of the Region of Waterloo formally requests the Province of Ontario to affirm and support the continued election of the Regional Chair by the voters of the Region of Waterloo or appointed by Region of Waterloo Council, And that the province be requested not to impose or advance legislation that would replace an elected chair with a provincially appointed position, And that the province be further requested to consult with the Region of Waterloo and its area municipalities prior to any proposed changes to the regional governance structure, And that a copy of this motion be forwarded to: The Premier of Ontario; The Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing; The Minister of Finance; All members of Provincial Parliament representing Waterloo Region; and The Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO).
motions.text_html:
The Administration and Finance Committee recommends as follows:

1.  That the Regional Municipality of Waterloo direct Facilities staff to explore the development of a Facilities Strategic Plan focused on the following five components:

    1. A complete inventory of all corporate facilities, including current usage, functional capacity, and condition;
    2. An analysis of operating and maintenance requirements and associated costs across all corporate facilities;
    3. A five- to ten-year capital outlook identifying required investments, lifecycle needs, and projected financial impacts;
    4. A review of accommodation standards and policies to support facilities planning and a demand analysis to clarify space needs;
    5. An evaluation of optimization opportunities, including consolidation, repurposing, or alternative service delivery options to ensure efficient and cost-effective use of corporate space;

And that staff report back to Council with the findings, options, and recommended next steps.

 

2.  The Council of the Region of Waterloo formally requests the Province of Ontario to affirm and support the continued election of the Regional Chair by the voters of the Region of Waterloo or appointed by Region of Waterloo Council,
And that the province be requested not to impose or advance legislation that would replace an elected chair with a provincially appointed position,
And that the province be further requested to consult with the Region of Waterloo and its area municipalities prior to any proposed changes to the regional governance structure,
And that a copy of this motion be forwarded to: 

    1. The Premier of Ontario;
    2. The Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing;
    3. The Minister of Finance;
    4. All members of Provincial Parliament representing Waterloo Region; and
    5. The Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO).

That staff of the Region of Waterloo be directed to report back to Council alongside the Water Supply Strategy in 2027 or sooner on measures available to protect and preserve the Region’s existing groundwater supply and associated wetlands, recognizing current water capacity constraints, long-term asset management planning and recent provincial legislative changes, including: an assessment of the effectiveness of existing Regional policies, designations, and development controls in protecting groundwater recharge areas, source water protection zones, wetlands, and moraine lands that contribute to the Region’s current water supply, and identification of any gaps or vulnerabilities; an evaluation of how land-use change within recharge areas and wetlands may affect groundwater availability, long-term water security, and future infrastructure requirements under existing growth scenarios; identification of opportunities for coordination with area municipalities and conservation authorities to improve alignment between source water protection science and land-use decision-making; consideration of precautionary or interim risk-mitigation measures that could reduce further stress on existing groundwater systems while remaining compliant with provincial legislation; identification of opportunities for coordination with area municipalities and conservation authorities to improve alignment between source water protection science and land-use decision-making; options for the Region to advocate to the Provincial Government for a provincially enabled “Bluebelt” or similar legislative framework to provide permanent protection for critical groundwater recharge areas, wetlands, and moraine lands beyond municipal authority, including an assessment of potential implications for growth management and infrastructure planning. And that the report be presented for information and discussion purposes, without prejudice, to future policy direction of Council. That the Regional Municipality of Waterloo direct staff to explore alternative service frequency models for the Region’s bulky item collection program, including: Monthly collection; Semi-monthly (every two months) collection; Semi-annual collection; And maintaining the current biweekly model as a baseline comparator. And that staff report back to Council by September 2026 including information on the Christmas Tree Bulk Item with: A comprehensive cost-benefit analysis of each model, including projected operational savings, fleet and staffing impacts, contract considerations, and administrative efficiencies. An assessment of environmental and community impacts, including potential changes to waste diversion, illegal dumping risks, and any required mitigation strategies. An analysis of resident experience implications, including accessibility and communication requirements. A recommended optimal scenario based on financial, operational, environmental, and community impacts. Options for phased implementation, pilot testing, or transition planning should Council consider changing the current service frequency. WHEREAS the Region of Waterloo has identified water supply capacity constraints within the Mannheim Service Area through its Water Supply Strategy update and associated third party technical review; and WHEREAS the Region’s existing methodology for determining remaining water supply capacity has been updated to reflect operational constraints, hydrological realities, and the need to maintain an operational resiliency buffer; and WHEREAS the Region has already established a risk-based approach to provide allocation of future unbuilt water and wastewater service capacity to enable growth (example: plans of subdivision) where the following criteria has been met: A capacity expansion project is imminent and included in the first five years of the Region’s 10year capital forecast, A sound technical basis exists for the anticipated capacity (supported by an Environmental Assessment, master plan, or equivalent engineering analysis), and Area Municipal recommendations guide approvals, with no more than 50% of projected new capacity allocated in advance of completion; and WHEREAS the Region has developed a preliminary list of initiatives to restore and increase capacity within the Mannheim Service Area; and WHEREAS municipal and industry partners have identified the urgent need for a clear, transparent, Regionwide allocation approach to ensure consistent interpretation of capacity constraints and development impacts across all area municipalities; and WHEREAS Waterloo Region continues to be in a housing supply crisis, particularly for lower income individuals within Waterloo Region; and WHEREAS according to the 2019 labour force survey 24,300 people are employed in construction which could be at risk. THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED: That Region staff be directed to work with Area Municipalities on a risk-based approach to advance the allocation of up to fifty per cent of planned and unbuilt capacity coming on-line within the next 5 years to support development approvals, in conjunction with restoring sustainable operating rates, and the minimum operational resiliency, consistent with the Region’s long-standing practice. That Regional staff work with Area Municipalities to develop and implement an enhanced water conservation program, including possible regulatory, pricing and incentive-based measures, to both mitigate peak system demands year-round and especially from May 1 – September 30 in order to enable restored and new water supply capacity to come online in parallel with continued development approvals as outlined in Recommendation 1.

motions.text: Whereas the Region of Waterloo is experiencing increasing constraints and uncertainty related to municipal water supply and capacity; and Whereas residents and the development industry have raised concerns regarding water sustainability, growth pressures and the availability of clear and transparent public information related to long term water planning; and Whereas a previous council motion authorized only staff level discussions with representatives of the Waterloo Home Builders Association, Build Urban, and the Grand Valley Construction Association regarding water supply constraints in an initial technical exchange; and Whereas water supply planning is a fundamental core public interest issue that requires direct engagement by Regional Council to ensure transparency, accountability and informed decision making. Therefore, be it resolved: That Regional Council direct staff to convene a one day working session involving regional council, relevant regional staff and invited representatives of the development industry including the Waterloo Home Builders association, Build Urban and the Grand Valley Construction Association to provide a comprehensive briefing on the Region’s water supply; and The working session be educational and informational in nature inviting commentary from both council and the development industry on water sustainability, growth pressures and the possibility of new guidelines on the staging of development; and Staff report back to council following the working session with a summary of key information presented, suggestions from the development industry on the staging of approvals and further recommended next steps for council.
motions.text_html:
Whereas the Region of Waterloo is experiencing increasing constraints and uncertainty related to municipal water supply and capacity; and

Whereas residents and the development industry have raised concerns regarding water sustainability, growth pressures and the availability of clear and transparent public information related to long term water planning; and

Whereas a previous council motion authorized only staff level discussions with representatives of the Waterloo Home Builders Association, Build Urban, and the Grand Valley Construction Association regarding water supply constraints in an initial technical exchange; and

Whereas water supply planning is a fundamental core public interest issue that requires direct engagement by Regional Council to ensure transparency, accountability and informed decision making.

Therefore, be it resolved:

  1. That Regional Council direct staff to convene a one day working session involving regional council, relevant regional staff and invited representatives of the development industry including the Waterloo Home Builders association, Build Urban and the Grand Valley Construction Association to provide a comprehensive briefing on the Region’s water supply; and
  2. The working session be educational and informational in nature inviting commentary from both council and the development industry on water sustainability, growth pressures and the possibility of new guidelines on the staging of development; and
  3. Staff report back to council following the working session with a summary of key information presented, suggestions from the development industry on the staging of approvals and further recommended next steps for council.

motions.text: WHEREAS all GRT riders start and end their journeys at a bus stop or station and expect reliable access to transit throughout the year, including during winter conditions; WHEREAS Winter 2025-2026 has seen increased winter operations and snow accumulation which has strained bus stop winter maintenance and accessibility, making it difficult for GRT riders to reliably access transit; THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the Commissioner of Transportation report to the Sustainability, Infrastructure, and Development Committee ahead of the Winter 2026-2027 season with: Options to enhance responsiveness of GRT bus stop winter maintenance service, including potential service level options and prioritization criteria; and Other opportunities to improve winter maintenance operations as part of the ongoing Area Maintenance Agreement review(s), in consultation with area municipalities.
motions.text_html:
WHEREAS all GRT riders start and end their journeys at a bus stop or station and expect reliable access to transit throughout the year, including during winter conditions;
 
WHEREAS Winter 2025-2026 has seen increased winter operations and snow accumulation which has strained bus stop winter maintenance and accessibility, making it difficult for GRT riders to reliably access transit;
 
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the Commissioner of Transportation report to the Sustainability, Infrastructure, and Development Committee ahead of the Winter 2026-2027 season with:

  1. Options to enhance responsiveness of GRT bus stop winter maintenance service, including potential service level options and prioritization criteria; and
  2. Other opportunities to improve winter maintenance operations as part of the ongoing Area Maintenance Agreement review(s), in consultation with area municipalities.

motions.text_html: That the Regional Municipality of Waterloo waive notice of motion as per section 70 of By-law 22-051, A By-law to Provide Rules for Governing the Proceedings of Council and its Committees, and to repeal By-Law 00-031, as amended.

motions.text: WHEREAS the Province of Ontario regulates Permits to Take Water (PTTW) under the Ontario Water Resources Act; AND WHEREAS the Region of Waterloo relies primarily on groundwater for its municipal drinking water supply; AND WHEREAS provincial data indicates there are currently 108 active PTTWs within the Region of Waterloo, authorizing a combined maximum taking of approximately 1.01 billion litres per day; AND WHEREAS within the Mannheim Service Area, there are 65 active permits authorizing approximately 740 million litres per day, of which 22 municipal permits account for approximately 472 million litres per day and 43 private permits account for approximately 268 million litres per day; AND WHEREAS recent groundwater capacity constraints identified within the Mannheim Service Area highlight the need for a precautionary and cumulative aquifer-level review of permitted water takings; THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT: The Region of Waterloo formally request that the Province of Ontario implement a temporary moratorium on the issuance or expansion of new private-sector Permits to Take Water within areas experiencing identified groundwater capacity constraints, including the Mannheim Service Area, until a cumulative aquifer-level impact review is completed; The Province undertake a regional cumulative groundwater impact assessment of all existing PTTWs within Waterloo Region, incorporating climate variability, drought resiliency, and projected population growth; The Province strengthen municipal engagement in the PTTW review process by requiring formal notification to affected municipalities of new, amended, or renewed PTTW applications; a defined municipal commenting period; and a written provincial response addressing municipal comments prior to final permit decisions; While the Province currently publishes a quarterly Permit to Take Water dataset, proactive notification and supporting documentation be provided directly to affected municipalities at the time of application submission and final decision; Enhanced annual public reporting be provided outlining permitted daily volumes by municipality; municipal versus private breakdowns; and aggregate actual annual takings compared to permitted maximums; This resolution be forwarded to the Minister of the Environment, Conservation and Parks; the Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing; local Members of Provincial Parliament; and the Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO).
motions.text_html:
WHEREAS the Province of Ontario regulates Permits to Take Water (PTTW) under the Ontario Water Resources Act;

AND WHEREAS the Region of Waterloo relies primarily on groundwater for its municipal drinking water supply;

AND WHEREAS provincial data indicates there are currently 108 active PTTWs within the Region of Waterloo, authorizing a combined maximum taking of approximately 1.01 billion litres per day;

AND WHEREAS within the Mannheim Service Area, there are 65 active permits authorizing approximately 740 million litres per day, of which 22 municipal permits account for approximately 472 million litres per day and 43 private permits account for approximately 268 million litres per day;

AND WHEREAS recent groundwater capacity constraints identified within the Mannheim Service Area highlight the need for a precautionary and cumulative aquifer-level review of permitted water takings;


THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT:

  1. The Region of Waterloo formally request that the Province of Ontario implement a temporary moratorium on the issuance or expansion of new private-sector Permits to Take Water within areas experiencing identified groundwater capacity constraints, including the Mannheim Service Area, until a cumulative aquifer-level impact review is completed;
  2. The Province undertake a regional cumulative groundwater impact assessment of all existing PTTWs within Waterloo Region, incorporating climate variability, drought resiliency, and projected population growth;
  3. The Province strengthen municipal engagement in the PTTW review process by requiring formal notification to affected municipalities of new, amended, or renewed PTTW applications; a defined municipal commenting period; and a written provincial response addressing municipal comments prior to final permit decisions;
  4. While the Province currently publishes a quarterly Permit to Take Water dataset, proactive notification and supporting documentation be provided directly to affected municipalities at the time of application submission and final decision;
  5. Enhanced annual public reporting be provided outlining permitted daily volumes by municipality; municipal versus private breakdowns; and aggregate actual annual takings compared to permitted maximums;
  6. This resolution be forwarded to the Minister of the Environment, Conservation and Parks; the Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing; local Members of Provincial Parliament; and the Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO).
